rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada and others identify the human here as Adam, drawn from clay.
rows.anchor: الإنسان هنا آدم عليه الصلاة والسلام قاله قتادة وغيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun refers to Adam’s descendant, omitted because the context is familiar and no other meaning fits; Qurtubi compares 38:32.
rows.anchor: وإن كان لم يذكر لشهرة الأمر فإن المعنى لا يصلح إلا له

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and others take sulāla as Adam’s descendant, here the distilled essence of fluid, meaning semen.
rows.anchor: المراد بالسلالة ابن آدم قاله ابن عباس وغيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sulāla derives from salla, extracting one thing from another; examples include drawing hair from dough and a sword from its sheath.
rows.anchor: السلالة فعالة من السل وهو استخراج الشيء من الشيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An anonymous poetic line calls offspring sulāla from a womb, illustrating extracted seed or lineage.
rows.anchor: فجاءت به عضب الأديم غضنفرا سلالة فرج كان غير حصين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another anonymous line calls Hind a purebred mare and a salīla of horses covered by a mule, illustrating descent.
rows.anchor: وما هند إلا مهرة عربية سليلة أفراس تجللها بغل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “From clay” means Adam’s origin is clay; his offspring come from clay and semen, as explained at the beginning of al-Anʿām.
rows.anchor: أي من طين خالص فأما ولده فهو من طين ومني

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi says sulāla is clay squeezed until it slips between the fingers; what emerges is called sulāla.
rows.anchor: السلالة الطين إذا عصرته انسل من بين أصابعك فالذي يخرج هو السلالة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi refers meanings and legal rulings about the drop, clot, and morsel to his earlier commentary on Sūrat al-Ḥajj.
rows.anchor: قد مضى القول في النطفة والعلقة والمضغة وما في ذلك من الأحكام في أول الحج

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, al-Shaʿbī, Abu al-ʿĀliya, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, and Ibn Zayd say the new creation is the breathing of the spirit into previously inert matter.
rows.anchor: ابن عباس والشعبي وأبو العالية والضحاك وابن زيد: هو نفخ الروح فيه بعد أن كان جمادا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A separate report from Ibn Abbas identifies the new creation as emergence into the world.
rows.anchor: ابن عباس: خروجه إلى الدنيا

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada transmits from a group that the phrase means the growth of the child’s hair.
rows.anchor: قتادة عن فرقة: نبات شعره

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says the phrase refers to teeth emerging and hair growing.
rows.anchor: الضحاك: خروج الأسنان ونبات الشعر

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid, also reported from Ibn Umar, interprets the phrase as reaching full youth.
rows.anchor: مجاهد: كمال شبابه وروي عن ابن عمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi prefers a general sense encompassing these stages and others: speech, perception, skill, acquiring intelligible knowledge, and development through death.
rows.anchor: والصحيح أنه عام في هذا وفي غيره من النطق والإدراك وحسن المحاولة وتحصيل المعقولات إلى أن يموت

rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
rows.claim: One report says Umar heard the passage through “a new creation,” uttered the closing phrase, and the Prophet replied that it was revealed that way.
rows.anchor: أن عمر بن الخطاب لما سمع صدر الآية إلى قوله: { خلقا آخر } قال فتبارك الله أحسن الخالقين

rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
rows.claim: In al-Ṭayālisī’s Musnad, Umar says he uttered the phrase when the creation passage was revealed, after which the matching verse was revealed.
rows.anchor: وفي مسند الطيالسي: ونزلت { ولقد خلقنا الإنسان من سلالة من طين } الآية فلما نزلت قلت أنا:

rows.speaker: معاذ بن جبل
rows.claim: Another report attributes the utterance to Muʿādh ibn Jabal.
rows.anchor: ويروى أن قائل ذلك معاذ بن جبل

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن أبي سرح
rows.claim: A report attributes the phrase to ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Sarḥ, who then apostatized, claiming he could produce what Muhammad produced; Qurtubi links the matter to 6:93.
rows.anchor: وروي أن قائل ذلك عبد الله بن أبي سرح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tabāraka is a derived form from baraka, blessing.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى «تبارك» تفاعل من البركة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aḥsan al-khāliqīn means the most exact or accomplished makers.
rows.anchor: { أحسن الخالقين } أتقن الصانعين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People may be called creators for manufacture; an anonymous poet contrasts completing what one makes with making but failing to finish it.
rows.anchor: يقال لمن صنع شيئا خلقه ومنه قول الشاعر: ولأنت تفري ما خلقت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some deny applying “creator” to people, reserving the word for God.
rows.anchor: وذهب بعض الناس إلى نفي هذه اللفظة عن الناس وإنما يضاف الخلق إلى الله تعالى

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj says God is the best of creators because He permitted Jesus to create.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن جريج: إنما قال: «أحسن الخالقين» لأنه تعالى قد أذن لعيسى عليه السلام أن يخلق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi allows “creating” for human manufacture but reserves creation from nothing for God.
rows.anchor: ولا تنفى اللفظة عن البشر في معنى الصنع وإنما هي منفية بمعنى الاختراع والإيجاد من العدم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: When Umar asked senior Companions about Laylat al-Qadr, Ibn Abbas reasoned from seven heavens, seven earths, Adam made from seven, and provision in seven that it was the twenty-seventh night; the long report is in Ibn Abī Shayba’s Musnad.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس لعمر حين سأل مشيخة الصحابة عن ليلة القدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi says Ibn Abbas meant this creation passage by Adam being made from seven; for the seven provisions he points to 80:27–31, while “ab” is for livestock.
rows.anchor: والأب للأنعام. والقضب يأكله ابن آدم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An unattributed view says humans eat qadb and that it fattens women.
rows.anchor: والقضب يأكله ابن آدم ويسمن منه النساء هذا قول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view defines qadb as cut greens, hence human food.
rows.anchor: القضب البقول لأنها تقضب فهي رزق ابن آدم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third view assigns qadb and ab to livestock, six listed items to humans, and the seventh to livestock as one of people’s greatest provisions.
rows.anchor: وقيل: القضب والأب للأنعام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tanfahu is a synonym of talfahu, as in 21:46, but talfahu conveys more intense torment; fire or scorching wind burns, while a sword’s lafḥa is a light blow.
rows.anchor: إلا أن «تلفح» أبلغ بأسا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses kāliḥūn as scowling; lexicographers describe the grimace as baring teeth with the lips drawn back.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: عابسون. وقال أهل اللغة: الكلوح تكشر في عبوس

rows.speaker: الأعشى
rows.claim: Al-Aʿshā’s line uses kalaḥ for a mouth whose cheek draws back from the tooth at the moment of struggle.
rows.anchor: قال الأعشى: وله المقدم لا مثل له ساعة الشدق عن الناب كلح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi notes forms kalaha, kulūḥan, and kalāḥan; kalḥa can mean the mouth and its surroundings, and a grim day is severe.
rows.anchor: وقد كلح الرجل كلوحا وكلاحا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas also describes them as one whose lips contract and whose pus flows.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس أيضا «وهم فيها كالحون» يريد كالذي كلح وتقلصت شفتاه وسال صديده

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd likens them to a scorched sheep’s head, with teeth exposed and lips contracted.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن مسعود: ألم تر إلى رأس المشيط بالنار

rows.speaker: أبو سعيد الخدري
rows.claim: Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī reports from the Prophet that fire shrinks the upper lip to mid-head and slackens the lower lip to the navel; al-Tirmidhī grades it ṣaḥīḥ gharīb.
rows.anchor: وفي الترمذي عن أبي سعيد الخدري عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God gave people homes for privacy and private enjoyment, forbade outsiders from looking in or entering without permission, and protected their seclusion and modesty.
rows.anchor: وحجر على الخلق أن يطلعوا على ما فيها من خارج أو يلجوها من غير إذن أربابها

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: Muslim reports from Abū Hurayra that a person who looks into a home without permission may have his eye gouged out.
rows.anchor: وفي صحيح مسلم عن أبي هريرة عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قال

rows.speaker: بعض العلماء
rows.claim: Some scholars say the eye-gouging report is not literal: the gouger would owe compensation and the report was abrogated by 16:126.
rows.anchor: فقال بعض العلماء: ليس هذا على ظاهره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another possibility treats the threat as a warning, not a binding rule; a report contradicting the Qurʾān cannot be acted upon.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن يكون خارج على وجه الوعيد لا على وجه الحتم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet’s reported order to Bilāl to “cut” ʿAbbās ibn Mirdās’s tongue after praise meant to give him something, not literally cut it.
rows.anchor: لما مدحه قال لبلال: «قم فاقطع لسانه» وإنما أراد بذلك أن يدفع إليه شيئا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The threat may figuratively mean imposing a consequence that prevents the intruder from looking into another home again.
rows.anchor: وكذلك هذا يحتمل أن يكون ذكر فقء العين والمراد أن يعمل به عمل حتى لا ينظر بعد ذلك في بيت غيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi’s preferred ruling is that the person who gouges the intruder’s eye owes neither compensation nor retaliation, relying on a report from Anas cited later.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم: لا ضمان عليه ولا قصاص وهو الصحيح إن شاء الله تعالى لحديث أنس

rows.speaker: عدي بن ثابت
rows.claim: A report from ʿAdī ibn Thābit says an Anṣārī woman asked how to prevent male relatives entering while she was in a state she did not want seen; the verse was revealed.
rows.anchor: عن عدي بن ثابت أن امرأة من الأنصار قالت:

rows.speaker: أبو بكر
rows.claim: Abū Bakr asked about unoccupied inns and roadside dwellings in Syria; 24:29 was then revealed to exempt uninhabited homes.
rows.anchor: الخانات والمساكن في طرق الشام

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Malik, as quoted by Ibn Wahb, says tastaʾnisū means seek permission; this wording is also attributed as a reading to Ubayy, Ibn Abbas, and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr.
rows.anchor: قال ابن وهب قال مالك: الاستئناس فيما نرى والله أعلم الاستئذان

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Another interpretation takes the word as finding out who is home; Mujahid says to clear the throat or otherwise signal, wait until noticed, then enter.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد: بالتنحنح أو بأي وجه أمكن

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī gives the sense of learning who is inside and supports it with 4:6, where ānastum means “you know.”
rows.anchor: وقال معناه الطبري ومنه قوله تعالى:

rows.speaker: أبو أيوب الأنصاري
rows.claim: A report in Ibn Mājah from Abū Ayyūb says the Prophet defined istī’nās as speaking a tasbīḥ, takbīr, or taḥmīd, clearing one’s throat, and notifying the household.
rows.anchor: عن أبي أيوب الأنصاري قال:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi says the Abū Ayyūb report plainly makes istī’nās distinct from asking permission, agreeing with Mujahid and those who share his view.
rows.anchor: وهذا نص في أن الاستئناس غير الاستئذان كما قال مجاهد ومن وافقه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A claim attributed to Ibn Abbas and others calls tastaʾnisū a scribal error for tastaʾdhinū; Qurtubi rejects this because the codices and Companion consensus preserve the received wording since ʿUthmān’s era.
rows.anchor: وروي عن ابن عباس وبعض الناس يقول عن سعيد بن جبير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi invokes 41:42 and 15:9 to argue the received Qurʾānic wording cannot be corrupted and the Companions’ agreed codices cannot be called erroneous.
rows.anchor: فهي التي لا يجوز خلافها

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report from Ibn Abbas, transmitted by Abū Ḥātim, proposes fronting and delaying: greet the household and then seek their notice.
rows.anchor: وقد روي عن ابن عباس أن في الكلام تقديما وتأخيرا

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya rejects that rearrangement: tastaʾnisū is clear Arabic, and Umar used it while standing at the Prophet’s room.
rows.anchor: ابن عطية: ومما ينفي هذا القول عن ابن عباس وغيره

rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
rows.claim: A well-known report has Umar at the Prophet’s room asking permission with the phrase astaʾnis, “May I seek your notice?”
rows.anchor: وقد قال عمر للنبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: أستأنس يا رسول الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: From the Abū Ayyūb report, Qurtubi concludes istī’nās precedes the greeting, so the verse remains in its stated order without transposition.
rows.anchor: قد ذكرنا من حديث أبي أيوب أن الاستئناس إنما يكون قبل السلام

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: The Sunnah is to ask permission three times and not exceed that; Malik allows another try only when certain the occupants did not hear.
rows.anchor: قال ابن وهب قال مالك: الاستئذان ثلاث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The visitor should greet and ask to enter, enter if allowed, leave if told to return, and depart after three unanswered requests.
rows.anchor: السلام عليكم أأدخل فإن أذن له دخل

rows.speaker: أبو موسى الأشعري
rows.claim: In the famous authentic report, Abū Mūsā told Umar he had greeted three times at his door without response and left; the Prophet instructed that an unanswered third request requires returning.
rows.anchor: وهو حديث مشهور أخرجه الصحيح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Three repetitions usually ensure speech is heard and understood; the Prophet repeated statements for comprehension and greeted people three times.
rows.anchor: إنما خص الاستئذان بثلاث لأن الغالب من الكلام إذا كرر ثلاثا سمع وفهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After three unanswered requests the host likely refuses or cannot answer; the visitor should leave rather than disturb or harm the host by insisting.
rows.anchor: فإذا لم يؤذن له بعد ثلاث ظهر أن رب المنزل لا يريد الإذن

rows.speaker: أبو أيوب
rows.claim: Qurtubi cites the Prophet telling Abū Ayyūb, who hurried out after seeking permission, “Perhaps we made you hurry,” illustrating the burden of insistence.
rows.anchor: قال النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم لأبي أيوب حين استأذن عليه فخرج مستعجلا

rows.speaker: ابن شهاب
rows.claim: Ibn Shihāb narrates that the Prophet greeted Saʿd ibn ʿUbāda three times and left without reply; Saʿd had heard and wanted more greetings, so he caught up and explained.
rows.anchor: وروى عقيل عن ابن شهاب قال: أما سنة التسليمات الثلاث

rows.speaker: ابن شهاب
rows.claim: Ibn Shihāb says the three greetings derive from the Saʿd incident; another Abū Dāwūd transmission includes Qays ibn Saʿd, while other transmitters give it mursal without Qays.
rows.anchor: قال ابن شهاب: فإنما أخذ التسليم ثلاثا من قبل ذلك

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas is reported to have said people abandoned asking permission; scholars suggest this followed the widespread use of doors and knocking.
rows.anchor: روي عن ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما أن الاستئذان ترك العمل به الناس

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن بسر
rows.claim: Abū Dāwūd reports from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Busr that the Prophet stood to a doorway’s right or left, not directly in front, and called out the greeting twice because homes then had no curtains.
rows.anchor: روى أبو داود عن عبد الله بن بسر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At a closed door one may stand where convenient and seek permission, or knock.
rows.anchor: فإن كان الباب مردودا فله أن يقف حيث شاء منه ويستأذن

rows.speaker: أبو موسى الأشعري
rows.claim: A report from Abū Mūsā says the Prophet was at a garden well when Abū Bakr knocked and was admitted with glad tidings of Paradise; Qurtubi judges the chain through ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Nāfiʿ sounder than al-Laythī’s variant.
rows.anchor: أبو موسى الأشعري: أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم كان في حائط بالمدينة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Knocking should be gentle enough to be heard and not forceful; Anas reports that the Prophet’s doors were tapped with fingernails.
rows.anchor: وصفة الدق أن يكون خفيفا بحيث يسمع

rows.speaker: جابر بن عبد الله
rows.claim: In both Ṣaḥīḥ collections, the Prophet asked Jābir who was there; Jābir said “I,” and the Prophet repeated “I, I!” in apparent disapproval.
rows.anchor: روى الصحيحان وغيرهما عن جابر بن عبد الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The scholars explain that “I” does not identify the visitor; one should say one’s name, as Umar and Abū Mūsā did.
rows.anchor: إنما كره النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم ذلك لأن قوله أنا لا يحصل بها تعريف

rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
rows.claim: Umar identified himself at the Prophet’s dwelling by greeting and asking whether Umar might enter; Muslim reports Abū Mūsā identifying himself to Umar as al-Ashʿarī.
rows.anchor: ثبت عن عمر بن الخطاب أنه أتى النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم وهو في مشربة له

rows.speaker: شعبة
rows.claim: When ʿAlī ibn ʿĀṣim answered “I” at Shuʿba’s door, Shuʿba joked that he had no friend named “I,” accompanying the report that the Prophet disliked that reply.
rows.anchor: منزل شعبة فدققت عليه الباب فقال: من هذا؟ قلت: أنا فقال: يا هذا ما لي صديق

rows.speaker: عمرو بن عبيد
rows.claim: At ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd’s door, the answer “I” prompted him to reply that only God knows the unseen.
rows.anchor: وذكر عن عمر بن شبة حدثنا محمد بن سلام عن أبيه

rows.speaker: علي بن المحسن
rows.claim: Al-Khaṭīb recounts ʿAlī ibn al-Muḥassin’s anecdote of a shaykh punning that “I” was the one who knocked.
rows.anchor: سمعت علي بن المحسن القاضي يحكي عن بعض الشيوخ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Each community may use its customary local expression when seeking permission.
rows.anchor: ثم لكل قوم في الاستئذان عرفهم في العبارة

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: A report has Abū Hurayra at a door asking “andar?” and being answered “andarun,” a Persian permission expression.
rows.anchor: إلى أبي هريرة فجاء معي

rows.speaker: أحمد بن صالح
rows.claim: Aḥmad ibn Ṣāliḥ says the Isfahani al-Darāwardī used “andarun” to invite entry in Medina, earning his nickname from it.
rows.anchor: أحمد بن صالح قال: كان الدراوردي من أهل أصبهان

rows.speaker: كلدة بن حنبل
rows.claim: Kalda ibn Ḥanbal entered the Prophet’s place in Mecca without greeting while delivering food from Ṣafwān ibn Umayya; the Prophet told him to return and greet, after Ṣafwān had become Muslim.
rows.anchor: روى أبو داود عن كلدة بن حنبل أن صفوان بن أمية بعثه

rows.speaker: أبو الزبير
rows.claim: Abū al-Zubayr reports from Jābir that the Prophet said not to admit someone who has not begun with the greeting.
rows.anchor: وروى أبو الزبير عن جابر أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: عطاء
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj reports that ʿAṭāʾ heard Abū Hurayra instruct that someone asking to enter without greeting be told to bring the key; when ʿAṭāʾ supplied the greeting, Abū Hurayra agreed.
rows.anchor: أخبرني عطاء قال: سمعت أبا هريرة يقول

rows.speaker: حذيفة
rows.claim: When a man looked into Ḥudhayfa’s home before asking, Ḥudhayfa said he had already entered with his eye but not with his backside.
rows.anchor: وروي أن حذيفة جاءه رجل

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: Abū Dāwūd reports that a messenger sent from one person to another constitutes permission; a related report says a meal invitation brought by a messenger also grants entry.
rows.anchor: أخرجه أبو داود أيضا عن أبي هريرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When eye contact occurs, the visitor owes the greeting, but being seen is not permission to enter; after greeting, ask and leave if refused.
rows.anchor: فإن وقعت العين على العين فالسلام قد تعين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These rules concern other people’s homes; in one’s own home with family present, permission is unnecessary but one should greet them.
rows.anchor: هذه الأحكام كلها إنما هي في بيت ليس لك

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says to greet the family when entering one’s own home, as they most deserve the greeting.
rows.anchor: قال قتادة: إذا دخلت بيتك فسلم على أهلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If one’s mother or sister is home, clear the throat or stamp one’s foot to alert them, since they may be in a state they would not want one to see.
rows.anchor: فإن كان فيه معك أمك أو أختك

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Ibn al-Qāsim reports Malik’s view that a man should seek permission before entering upon his mother or sister.
rows.anchor: قال ابن القاسم قال مالك: ويستأذن الرجل على أمه وأخته

rows.speaker: عطاء بن يسار
rows.claim: A report says the Prophet told a man to seek permission to enter upon his mother even though he served her, asking if he would like to see her naked.
rows.anchor: وقد روى عطاء بن يسار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Scholars prescribe a formula invoking peace and blessed greetings when entering one’s empty home; the report via Ibn Wahb from the Prophet has a weak chain.
rows.anchor: فقال علماؤنا: يقول السلام علينا

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says to greet oneself and God’s righteous servants in an empty home, and relates that angels answer.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: إذا دخلت بيتا ليس فيه أحد

rows.speaker: ابن العربي
rows.claim: Ibn al-ʿArabī says the sound position is to omit greeting and permission in an empty home; Qurtubi considers Qatada’s view good.
rows.anchor: قال ابن العربي: والصحيح ترك السلام والاستئذان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One parsing makes in yattakhidhūnaka the response to idhā; another leaves the response implicit (“they said/say this one...”) and treats the clause as parenthetical.
rows.anchor: جواب { إذا } { إن يتخذونك } لأن معناه يتخذونك

rows.speaker: أبو جهل
rows.claim: The verse was revealed about Abū Jahl, who mocked the Prophet by asking whether this was the person God sent as messenger.
rows.anchor: ونزلت في أبي جهل كان يقول للنبي صلى الله عليه وسلم مستهزئا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The relative clause omits its object; rasūlan is accusative as a circumstantial phrase, meaning “sent as a messenger.”
rows.anchor: والعائد محذوف، أي بعثه الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A-hādhā is the subject and alladhī its predicate; baʿatha is in the relative clause and God is its nominative subject.
rows.anchor: رفع بالابتداء و { الذي } خبره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, rasūlan may be a verbal noun, meaning “a message,” since baʿatha means “sent.”
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون مصدرا لأن معنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The interrogative hamza conveys a taunt meant to belittle.
rows.anchor: والألف للاستفهام على معنى التقرير والاحتقار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The mockers say Muhammad nearly turned them away from their idols, had they not held fast to their worship.
rows.anchor: أي قالوا قد كاد أن يصرفنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They will learn at the punishment who is more astray, they or Muhammad; Qurtubi says they saw it at Badr.
rows.anchor: يريد من أضل دينا أهم أم محمد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God tells the Prophet to marvel that they persist in shirk despite acknowledging Him as creator and provider, then worship a stone without proof.
rows.anchor: عجب نبيه صلى الله عليه وسلم من إضمارهم على الشرك وإصرارهم عليه مع إقرارهم بأنه خالقهم ورازقهم

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī and others say an Arab who desired something worshipped it, then abandoned it for a better-looking object; the preposition is omitted and the sense is “a god according to his desire.”
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي وغيره: كانت العرب إذا هوي الرجل منهم شيئا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says desire itself is an idol worshipped apart from God, and recited the verse as evidence.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: الهوى إله يعبد من دون الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view means he obeys his desire; al-Ḥasan says he follows anything he desires, which Qurtubi regards as the same sense.
rows.anchor: وقيل: { اتخذ إلهه هواه } أي أطاع هواه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An anonymous poem imagines an ascetic praying to a woman before praying to God, illustrating desire redirecting worship.
rows.anchor: لصلى لها قبل الصلاة لربه ولا ارتد في الدنيا بأعمال فاتك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A wakīl would guard or guarantee a return to faith and rescue from corruption; guidance is not the Prophet’s choice, whose duty is to convey.
rows.anchor: أي حفيظا وكفيلا حتى ترده إلى الإيمان وتخرجه من هذا الفساد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi calls the passage a rebuttal to the Qadariyya.
rows.anchor: وهذا رد على القدرية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view says the verse was abrogated by the fighting verse; another says it remains as consolation for the Prophet.
rows.anchor: ثم قيل: إنها منسوخة بآية القتال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Poetic examples permit an omitted noun when removing it leaves the sense intact; likewise “their necks remained” means they remained humbled before it. Al-Farrāʾ and Abū ʿUbayda rely on this analysis.
rows.anchor: وإنما أجاز ذلك لأنه لو أسقط مر وطول من الكلام لم يفسد معناه

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisāʾī parses the phrase as “its necks are humbled, namely they themselves”; Basran grammarians and al-Farrāʾ call this wrong.
rows.anchor: والكسائي يذهب إلى أن المعنى خاضعيها هم

rows.speaker: النحاس
rows.claim: Al-Naḥḥās objects that this kind of ellipsis does not occur in ordinary speech.
rows.anchor: ومثل هذا الحذف لا يقع في شيء من الكلام قاله النحاس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi says he discussed the phrase about new reminders in Sūrat al-Anbiyāʾ.
rows.anchor: تقدم في «الأنبياء»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who turn away from a message and do not accept it have thereby denied it.
rows.anchor: أي أعرضوا ومن أعرض عن شيء ولم يقبله فهو تكذيب له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This is a threat: mockers will face the consequences of what they rejected and ridiculed.
rows.anchor: وعيد لهم أي فسوف يأتيهم عاقبة ما كذبوا والذي استهزءوا به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Growth on earth displays God’s greatness and power; those who looked with insight would know that only He deserves worship.
rows.anchor: نبه على عظمته وقدرته وأنهم لو رأوا بقلوبهم ونظروا ببصائرهم

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ glosses zawj as a kind or color.
rows.anchor: والزوج هو اللون قاله الفراء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Karīm means beautiful and noble; the root denotes honor and merit, and describes excellent, fruitful palms and virtuous, forgiving people.
rows.anchor: وأصل الكرم في اللغة الشرف والفضل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nabata and anbata both mean to grow or cause growth; God is the one who brings forth the plants.
rows.anchor: ونبتت الأرض وأنبتت بمعنى

rows.speaker: الشعبي
rows.claim: Al-Shaʿbī says people are plants of the earth: those destined for Paradise are noble and those for the Fire are lowly.
rows.anchor: عن الشعبي أنه قال: الناس من نبات الأرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Earth’s vegetation is a sign that God is capable of all things and nothing can thwart Him.
rows.anchor: أي فيما ذكر من الإنبات في الأرض لدلالته على أن الله قادر

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Most did not affirm the truth God already knew about them; Sibawayh treats kāna as extra here, equivalent to “most of them did not believe.”
rows.anchor: و { كان } هنا صلة في قول سيبويه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is invincible and avenges His enemies, while showing mercy to His allies.
rows.anchor: يريد المنيع المنتقم من أعدائه
